sounds.name: Follow the Drinkin' Gourd Karaoke Key of Dm - R. Smith Music (128k).mp3

captions.text: My name is Liza. People on this road call me Auntie Liza.
Drink before we go anywhere.
We have a long road ahead.
Do you see that quilt out there? In that window.
That is a message. Someone hung it there for someone exactly like you, tonight.
Every pattern on that cloth means something. I am going to teach you how to read them.
But first, if you seek freedom, let it know you are ready. Raise your hands or say freedom
There it is.
That one - the Crossroads. That is where we are headed. Point to it with me.
Good. Remember that shape.
We are not going back to this place. Not tonight. Not ever.
The first time I walked this road, I stood at a crossroads just like this one and I could not move.
Not from fear. But because I had never in my life made a choice that was only mine to make.
That is what the Crossroads pattern means. Not a junction in the road but the moment you stop waiting for someone else to decide for you.
The Crossroads pattern was first named for Cleveland. A real city, a crossroads where many different routes to Canada come together.
Two paths. I know what is on both of them. Neither is easy and both go north.
Choose where you are going. Point to it.
No going back. Don’t be nervous, that is not a bad thing.
No going back. Don’t be nervous, that is not a bad thing.
Look up.
Those birds have been flying north every spring since before any of our families were brought to this land. They don’t need a map. They just go.
The Flying Geese pattern was hung to say: follow what nature is showing you. The birds know where water is. When you are lost and the road is gone - look up. They will be there.
Track where they are going.
North. That direction, right there.
Do you see the path they travel? There is water below that flight line. Always is. Point it out - we will need it.
Good.
North. Say it again when you are tired. It helps.
We are moving through Ohio now. The border is not far, let’s keep moving.
I need to tell you something.
If we get separated - and I pray we do not - this is how you find north without me.
That star at the top of the sky. The one that is not moving while everything else turns. That is Polaris. The North Star.
Every other star rises and sets. That one never moves. It has been there for everyone who ever needed it.
There was a song - Follow the Drinking Gourd - passed around in work songs, in whispers.
Hidden in the words was a map of the sky.
The Big Dipper points straight to Polaris, every time. Without fail.
Show me the gourd first. Four stars for the bowl, three for the handle.
Follow where the water would pour out. Where does it point?
Draw the star yourself. One finger.
That is yours. Say “follow the gourd”
Yes. The people who sang that song were singing a map. You just sang it.
Point your arm toward it and hold.
That star will never move. And now you know how to find it.
Wherever you end up - you know which way is north.
Rest if you can. Tomorrow will ask everything of us.
The Monkey Wrench pattern said: gather your tools. Greater than what your hands can carry.
I have seen people leave with so much they could not move fast enough.
We are going to be deliberate about this now.
Look at what we have.
Three days of food, pressed flat so it does not show. Hover over it.
Rope. Thin - for water crossings. You do not know yet when you will need it. That is exactly why we take it.
Dark cloth. For your face and hands at night. You become part of the dark. Shadow does not get caught.
The lantern.
Use it only when you must. The dark is your protection on this road. But when you need to see - this.
And this last gift you cannot hold in your hand.
Everything you have learned about the quilt codes. Every pattern. It lives in you now. Touch your own head.
No one can search you for that. No one can take it off you.
That is the most important thing you are carrying.
There is a house about a mile ahead. I know the person inside. They are expecting us.
That pattern - the Shoofly. That means this is a safe house.
Someone inside decided the risk was worth it. Decided that strangers on the road were worth their life to help.
The Underground Railroad is not a thing.
But the knock has to be right. Three beats - short, short, long.
Check the road.
Now knock.
Hold still. Hands open. Let them see you.
Take it.
You may never know that person's name. But they opened that door.
The conductor says we are two days from the Niagara River.
There are people working out of St. Catharines, on the other side of that river. They have brought many people across.
Good news - we are off their road.
Bad news - we are off every road.
But look at the ground.
Bear prints.  The Bear's Paw pattern said: follow the animal trail.
We follow what they left. The land knows more than we do.
Reach out and trace the trail.
It’s what your mind knows and what you can hold onto when everything else is stripped away.
And I have seen people leave with nothing but their own name and make it through.
Water first. Already done.
Take it when you are ready.
It is people. Hundreds of them, in houses like this one, on roads like this one, who said: come in. I have you.
The next stretch is through the wilderness - it's the safest way.
Off their roads means off their maps.
Bears know where water is, where food grows, where shelter is in the cold.
Before any road was ever cut through this forest, they had already mapped it.
Keep with it.
Fork here. Which way do the prints go?
Other way. Look again.
Other way. Look again.
Good. Keep moving.
Water. Right there. Just like the bear prints showed us.
There is a town ahead. And in that town we cannot look like what we are.
Hamilton. A working town; wagons, merchants, people moving.
The Bow Tie pattern meant: change what you look like. Right now.
Hundreds of people passed through checkpoints like this one by looking like someone else.
The patrol does not see who is walking toward them. They see what they are shown.
Hat first.
Now the coat.
Stand straight. Shoulders back.
Ready?
Then walk like you mean it.
The conductor arranged a wagon on the other side of town. We just have to get to it.
We can move through it if we look like we belong.
We are going to be very careful about what that is.
This is the posture of someone who belongs exactly where they are going.
There it is. Right where she said.
The Wagon Wheel meant: prepare to travel by wagon.
Both ways have worked. Both have kept people alive.
Check the road.
Clear. Now choose.
Some of these were built with compartments underneath, for exactly this purpose.
Others were just a wagon on a road where wagons belonged.
No right answer - only the one that keeps you moving.
Under the boards. Still as you have ever been.
Any sound from under there is a sound you cannot take back.
That kind of stillness is its own kind of strength.
Stay sharp. Something has changed - I can feel it.
Stay low. Move with the wagon.
Every turn is a mile closer. We are getting there.
Stay sharp. Something has changed - I can feel it.
Let the wheels set the pace. You are just cargo that walks.
Stop.
Listen.
That is the signal. Someone is on that road who should not be.
That is the signal. Someone is on that road who should not be.
Listen.
Pack everything. Now.
Faster!
Leave nothing. Nobody was ever here.
Go.
Run!
I can hear it. Do you hear it?
That is the Conestogo. We are almost there. Come on.
The Conestogo River.
Wellington County, Ontario.
Every time I have stood here, I have thought: this is it. This is what we were walking toward.
On the other side of this river is the Queen's Bush.
A stretch of land nobody else wanted. And because nobody else wanted it, people came and built something extraordinary.
Starting around 1820, more than fifteen hundred free and formerly enslaved Black people arrived here. They cleared this wilderness.
That is what is waiting across this water.
Look back before we cross. One last time.
Everyone who walked that road before you. Everyone who will walk it after. You carry them when you cross.
The rope you've packed - take it out.
There is the boat. Throw the rope.
Row. Slow and steady.
Hold still. Feel the current.
Finally, we're here on free soil.
Spread your arms. Take it all in.
Queen's Bush. Wellington County. Canada. Yours.
They did not stop walking.
Neither will you.
This history still stands. And you are part of it now.
They built farms. Churches. Schools. They named their children here and buried their elders here.
Good. Now, launch it.
